title: JOSHUA HAD HIS SWORD READY… UNTIL ONE WORD FROM A STRANGER BROUGHT HIM TO HIS KNEES
paragraphs: JOSHUA HAD HIS SWORD READY… UNTIL ONE WORD FROM A STRANGER BROUGHT HIM TO HIS KNEES
There was a sword in the Stranger’s hand.
And Joshua had no idea whose side He was on.
Think about that for a moment.

Joshua was not some inexperienced soldier trembling at the sight of danger. He had fought battles. He had witnessed miracles. He had stood beside Moses. He had seen what happened when the living God moved on behalf of His people.
But this was different.
Moses was gone.
The responsibility was now on Joshua’s shoulders.
Behind him stood an entire nation depending on his leadership. Before him stood Jericho, a fortified city whose walls seemed to mock every promise God had made.
And somewhere between the weight of yesterday’s losses and tomorrow’s impossible battle, Joshua encountered someone he could not identify.
A Man.
Standing before him.
With a drawn sword.
Joshua approached Him and asked a question that made perfect sense to a military commander.
“Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?” (Joshua 5:13, KJV).
In other words…
Are You here to help us? Or have You come to destroy us?
The answer should have been simple.
Israel was God's covenant people. God had promised them the land. Jericho stood in the way. Surely anyone sent from heaven would declare allegiance to Israel.
But the Stranger gave an answer Joshua probably never expected.
“Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come.” (Joshua 5:14, KJV).
No.
Not yes.
Not a reassuring declaration of loyalty to Joshua's military campaign.
No.
And that single word shattered the assumptions behind Joshua's question.
Because the greatest issue at Jericho was never whether God would join Joshua's side.
It was whether Joshua would submit himself to God's command.
And perhaps that is where this ancient encounter begins speaking directly into the places we would rather keep hidden.
Because we have all stood before our own Jericho.
A marriage that feels impossible to repair.
A diagnosis that changes everything.
A family member who no longer wants anything to do with God.
A betrayal that still burns when everyone thinks we have moved on.
A financial crisis we cannot pray away overnight.
A private addiction that has survived every promise we made to stop.
A calling that frightens us because we know we are not strong enough to accomplish it ourselves.
And somewhere in the middle of those battles, we pray:
“Lord, are You on my side?”
But what if the question we desperately need to ask is something far more searching?
“Lord, am I surrendered to You?”
That distinction changes everything.
To understand why, we need to return to the ground where Joshua stood.
The Hebrew text of Joshua 5:13 records his question:
הֲלָנוּ אַתָּה אִם־לְצָרֵינוּ
Halanu attah im-letsareinu?
“Are you for us, or for our adversaries?”
The question is direct. Joshua wants to know where this armed figure stands in relation to the conflict.
But the reply begins with a striking Hebrew word:
לֹא — Loʾ
“No.”
Then the Stranger identifies Himself:
אֲנִי שַׂר־צְבָא־יְהוָה עַתָּה בָאתִי
Ani sar-tseva-YHWH attah vati.
“I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come.”
The Hebrew title sar-tseva-YHWH means “commander of the army of the LORD.”
The word sar refers to a ruler, prince, or commander. Tseva refers to an army or host, and YHWH is the divine covenant name of the LORD.
This was no ordinary soldier wandering near Jericho.
Joshua was standing before the Commander of the LORD's army.
And notice what the Commander did not say.
He did not say that God's purposes were unconnected to Israel. Scripture had already made clear that the LORD had promised to give Jericho into Israel's hands (Joshua 6:2).
Nor was He suggesting that truth and evil were morally interchangeable.
The issue was authority.
Joshua had approached as a commander attempting to identify a potential ally or enemy.
But he discovered that he was standing before an authority infinitely greater than his own.
The man who thought he needed to determine the Stranger's allegiance was about to discover that his own allegiance was the question that mattered.
And Joshua's response was extraordinary.
He fell facedown.
He bowed.
And he asked:
“What saith my lord unto his servant?” (Joshua 5:14, KJV).
Read that again.
He did not ask for the Stranger's military credentials.
He did not demand an explanation.
He did not begin listing Israel's qualifications for divine assistance.
He fell before Him and offered himself as a servant.
The Hebrew expression is equally powerful:
מָה אֲדֹנִי מְדַבֵּר אֶל־עַבְדּוֹ
Mah adoni medabber el-avdo?
“What is my lord saying to his servant?”
Joshua's posture had changed.
Moments earlier, he was asking the Stranger to identify His position.
Now Joshua was asking for instructions.
And that is where genuine surrender begins.
Not when God finally agrees to the future we have planned.
Not when He removes every obstacle.
Not when He answers our prayers exactly as we imagined.
But when we come before Him and say:
“Lord, even if Your answer is different from what I want, I belong to You.”
There is something painfully personal about this.
Because many of us want the protection of God without the correction of God.
We want His promises, but we struggle with His commands.
We want Him to defeat our enemies, but we become uncomfortable when His Word exposes the enemy of pride living inside our own hearts.
We want God to bless our decisions, even when we never stopped to ask whether those decisions honored Him.
We want Jesus as Savior, but we sometimes resist His authority as Lord.
And then we wonder why surrender feels so difficult.
Maybe because surrender requires something our pride has spent years protecting.
Control.
Joshua had to release his control before Jericho's walls ever fell.
But there is another detail in this encounter that makes the entire scene even more astonishing.
The Commander spoke again.
And His next instruction had nothing to do with siege weapons, battle formations, or military intelligence.
He said:
“Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy.” (Joshua 5:15, KJV).
Holy ground.
Outside Jericho.
In the shadow of an approaching war.
Does that sound familiar?
Years earlier, Moses encountered God at the burning bush and heard a remarkably similar command.
“Put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.” (Exodus 3:5, KJV).
The parallel is unmistakable.
Moses stood before God at the beginning of his commission to deliver Israel from Egypt.
Now Joshua stood before the Commander of the LORD's army as Israel prepared to enter a decisive new stage of possessing the promised land.
Both encounters involved the removal of sandals.
Both involved holy ground.
Both confronted a human leader with the overwhelming reality of divine presence and authority.
And both reminded God's servant that the mission belonged to the LORD before it belonged to the man.
The holiness of that ground did not come from its geography.
It came from the presence of the Holy One.
That matters more than we may realize.
Because we often assume that God's presence is most clearly revealed when our circumstances become comfortable.
When the bills are paid.
When the family is healthy.
When the prayers are answered.
When the doors finally open.
But Joshua encountered holy ground while an enormous enemy stronghold still stood in front of him.
The walls had not fallen.
The battle had not been fought.
The danger had not disappeared.
Yet God was already making His presence known.
Sometimes the holiest moments of your life will not happen after the battle is over.
They will happen while you are still standing in front of the walls, wondering how you could possibly survive what comes next.
And perhaps someone reading this right now understands that better than anyone else.
You have been asking God to remove something.
But He has been teaching you to trust Him while it remains.
You have been praying for an immediate escape.
But He has been calling you into deeper obedience.
You have been begging for certainty about tomorrow.
But He has been asking you to be faithful today.
That does not mean every hardship was personally sent by God to teach you a lesson. Scripture does not permit us to make that assumption about every suffering person.
It does mean that God's people can trust His faithfulness even when they cannot understand His timing.
And sometimes the greatest miracle begins before anything around us changes.
It begins when our hearts bow.
But now we must face a question that Christians have wrestled with for centuries.
Who was this mysterious Commander?
Was He an angel?
Was He a visible manifestation of God?
Was this an appearance of the eternal Son of God before His incarnation?
We must be careful here, because reverence for Scripture includes refusing to claim certainty where Scripture does not explicitly give it.
Joshua 5 identifies the figure as the Commander of the LORD's army. It does not explicitly name Him as Jesus Christ.
Many Christian interpreters have understood this encounter as a Christophany, a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son of God.
They point to Joshua's act of bowing, the command concerning holy ground, and the close connection between this appearance and the LORD's speech in Joshua 6.
Other faithful interpreters understand the figure as an exalted heavenly messenger representing God's authority.

The Hebrew verb describing Joshua's bowing, shachah, can refer to worship or to reverential prostration, depending on context. By itself, therefore, it does not conclusively establish the figure's identity.
The command concerning holy ground strongly evokes a divine encounter, but the precise identity of the Commander remains a matter of interpretation.
What we can say with confidence is that Joshua was being confronted with the authority and holiness of the LORD.
And when we read this account within the full testimony of Scripture, its deepest theological themes lead us toward Jesus Christ.
Not because we need to force His name into a verse that does not explicitly contain it.
But because the New Testament reveals Him as the One through whom God's saving purposes reach their fulfillment.
Jesus is the risen Lord to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given (Matthew 28:18).
He is the One before whom every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9–11).
He is the One who calls His disciples not merely to admire Him, but to follow Him.
And in Revelation 19:11–16, the victorious Christ is portrayed as the faithful and true King who judges in righteousness.
There is a sword associated with His victory.
There is authority no earthly army can overthrow.
There is a kingdom no wall can keep out.
But we must never confuse the military conquest of ancient Jericho with a command for Christians to wage physical violence in Christ's name today.
Jesus declared that His kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36).
The apostles taught that the weapons of Christian warfare are not fleshly (2 Corinthians 10:3–5).
Our calling is not to conquer people by force.
It is to bear witness to Christ, proclaim the Gospel, resist sin, love our enemies, and stand faithfully in the truth.
And here is where the story becomes even more personal.
Joshua stood before Jericho with a sword in his hand.
But Jesus went to Calvary and willingly endured the violence of sinful humanity.
Joshua faced a city whose walls needed to fall.
Jesus faced the judgment our sins deserved so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
Joshua was called to obey the LORD in a particular moment of Israel's history.
Jesus obeyed the Father perfectly, even unto death on a cross (Philippians 2:8).
And through His resurrection, He accomplished a victory that no earthly military conquest could ever achieve.
Victory over sin and death.
That is the Gospel.
Not that Jesus came to endorse every side we choose.
Not that He came to make every ambition successful.
Not that following Him guarantees an easy life.
But that the sinless Son of God died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He came to save sinners.
People whose stories are stained by decisions they cannot undo.
People whose reputations have collapsed.
People who have hurt others.
People who have been hurt by others.
People who have spent years pretending they are spiritually stronger than they really are.
People who know the language of worship but have forgotten the tenderness of repentance.
People like us.
And that brings us to a truth that can be difficult to accept.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the story we were writing. He came to redeem us and make us new.
It reflects the transforming power of the Gospel.
The scandal of human sin is real.
The guilt is real.
The consequences can be devastating.
And grace does not pretend otherwise.
But the mercy of God in Jesus Christ is also real.
The cross is real.
The empty tomb is real.
And the promise of new life is real.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV).
Notice the promise.
It does not say that every consequence of the past instantly disappears.
It does not say that damaged relationships automatically heal without truth, repentance, and patient restoration.
It does not say that becoming a Christian removes every temptation or struggle.
It says that those who are in Christ are made new.
Their relationship with God is transformed.
Their identity is no longer defined by condemnation.
And the Holy Spirit begins the lifelong work of making them more like Jesus.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain in rebellion.
Not a religious disguise for an unchanged heart.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that teaches us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
Grace that brings the proud to their knees and lifts the repentant into the mercy of Christ.
Maybe you have spent years trying to convince everyone that you are okay.
You smile in church.
You share Bible verses.
You tell people God is good.
And He is.
But somewhere beneath that smile is a battle nobody knows about.
Maybe your marriage is barely surviving.
Maybe your children are far from the faith you tried to teach them.
Maybe your prayer life has become little more than exhausted whispers.
Maybe you have returned to the same sin so many times that you are ashamed to ask for forgiveness again.
And perhaps the most frightening thought in your heart is this:
“What if God has finally had enough of me?”
Listen carefully.
The answer to that fear is not found in pretending your sin is harmless.
It is found in looking to Jesus Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9, KJV).
And Jesus Himself said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV).
These are not promises that excuse deliberate rebellion.
They are invitations to genuine repentance and faith.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect spiritual record before coming to Christ.
You come because you need the Savior.
You confess because He is merciful.
You turn from sin because His grace is too precious to treat casually.
And you follow because the One who died for you is worthy of your entire life.
Joshua did not become stronger than Jericho by falling on his face.
He acknowledged the authority of the One who was greater than Jericho.
And maybe that is what you need today.
Not another motivational speech telling you how powerful you are.
Not another promise that everything will work out exactly as you want.
Not another religious performance designed to convince people you have everything together.
Maybe you need to kneel before the Lord and tell Him the truth.
“Jesus, I have been trying to control everything.”
“I have been defending things You are calling me to surrender.”
“I have been asking You to bless decisions I made without seeking You.”
“I have been more concerned about winning arguments than reflecting Your character.”
“I have wanted Your help, but I have resisted Your correction.”
“Lord, forgive me.”
That kind of prayer may not impress the world.
But Scripture tells us:
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.” (James 4:6, KJV).
And there is something beautiful about a person who finally stops pretending.
A father admitting he needs to apologize to his children.
A wife or husband choosing honesty instead of another season of hidden resentment.
A young believer confessing a secret sin and seeking trustworthy spiritual accountability.
A church leader remembering that ministry is not a personal kingdom.
A Christian who has wandered far from prayer opening the Bible again with trembling hands.
A person who has never truly trusted Christ finally calling upon Him for salvation.
These moments may never trend online.
But they matter before God.
Because repentance is not spiritual humiliation for its own sake.
It is the turning of a sinner toward the mercy and authority of Jesus Christ.
And the most remarkable thing about Joshua's encounter is what happened afterward.
The LORD gave Joshua instructions that would have sounded absurd according to ordinary military strategy.
March around the city.
Carry the ark.
Have the priests blow trumpets.
Follow the appointed pattern.
Then, at the appointed time, shout.
Read Joshua 6 carefully.
Israel was not instructed to trust in superior weapons or human ingenuity.
The victory was presented as the LORD's gift, received through obedient faith.
Hebrews 11:30 later declares:
“By faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they were compassed about seven days.”
By faith.
Not by arrogance.
Not by spiritual showmanship.
Not by treating God like a tool for accomplishing personal ambitions.
By faith.
And faith in Scripture is not merely believing that something good will happen.
It is trusting the God who has spoken.
Even when obedience does not look impressive.
Even when the waiting feels unbearable.
Even when the outcome is beyond our control.
That is why the lesson of Joshua's encounter is not simply, “God will knock down every wall in your life.”
That would be a comforting slogan, but it would go beyond what this passage promises.
Some obstacles are removed.
Some trials endure.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Some faithful believers suffer deeply and never receive the earthly outcome they longed for.
Yet Christ remains Lord.
His resurrection remains true.
His grace remains sufficient.
And His promise never to abandon His people remains secure.
The greatest victory God offers us is not a life without trouble.
It is reconciliation with Himself through Jesus Christ and the certain hope of eternal life.
So perhaps the question is not whether your Jericho will fall tomorrow.
Perhaps the question is whether you will trust Jesus today.
Will you obey Him when no one is watching?
Will you forgive when bitterness feels more satisfying?
Will you confess when hiding seems safer?
Will you make things right where repentance requires restitution or an apology?
Will you remain faithful when obedience costs you something?
Will you follow Christ even when He refuses to become a servant of your personal agenda?
Because Joshua's question still echoes across the centuries.
“Are You for us, or for our enemies?”
And the Lord's authority still confronts every generation.
We do not get to recruit God into our pride, prejudice, selfish ambition, or self-righteousness.
We are called to surrender to Him.
Even our religious pride.
Even our desire to appear victorious.
Even our tendency to confuse our personal preferences with the will of God.
Especially those things.
And before you move on, I want to ask you something that deserves more than a casual answer.
What is the Jericho standing in front of you right now?
Not necessarily the problem you want God to remove.
But the place where you are struggling to trust and obey Him.
Is it fear?
Unforgiveness?
A hidden sin?
The need to control everything?
The shame of your past?
The exhaustion of trying to appear spiritually strong?
Someone may need to hear that Jesus has not stopped working in the lives of imperfect people.
Not because your story makes you the hero.
But because His mercy deserves the glory.
There is also someone in your life who may need this message more than you realize.
The friend who has quietly stopped attending church.
The parent carrying the pain of a wandering child.
The brother or sister who feels defeated by recurring temptation.
The person who believes their past is too scandalous for grace.
The unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because the Gospel is worth making known.
And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, I invite you to become part of this growing community of believers and seekers who want more than inspirational religious content.
We want to open Scripture.
We want to understand what it actually says.
We want to confront the uncomfortable truths we would rather avoid.
We want to grow in repentance, faith, holiness, grace, and love.
We want our families and friends to know Jesus Christ.
And we want every story of redemption to point back to the Savior, not to ourselves.
That is also why I want to invite you to consider something deeper than simply reading another article.
There is a real difference between consuming Christian content and choosing to help make faithful Christian teaching available to others.
Every article requires time, study, writing, and care.
Every resource made available freely represents an opportunity for someone to encounter biblical truth.
We cannot know how God will use any particular article.
But we can be faithful with the opportunities He places before us.

For Christians who are prayerfully considering their giving, such support can be a voluntary ministry offering. It should not, however, be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe or treated as a replacement for responsibilities to one's local church, family, or other commitments.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and joyful:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV).
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
Not by suggesting that God's approval can be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for financial support (Ephesians 2:8–9).

But if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, drawn you closer to Christ, encouraged you through difficult seasons, or equipped you to share the Gospel with others, consider becoming one of the people who help sustain it.
These products are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
These free resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and spiritual growth accessible to more people.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Share the Gospel.
Your prayers, thoughtful comments, testimonies, and willingness to share biblical truth also matter.
Jesus Christ is worthy.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not any writer.
Not any ministry platform.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who forgives repentant sinners.
The One who calls His people to holiness.
The One who turns the ashamed toward grace, the wandering toward repentance, and the spiritually dead toward new life.
And now, before you close this article, I want you to return one last time to that scene outside Jericho.
Imagine the dust beneath Joshua's feet.
The silent city walls in the distance.
The weight of thousands of lives resting upon his leadership.
The armed Stranger standing before him.
The drawn sword.
The question.
“Are You for us, or for our enemies?”
And then that unexpected answer.
“No.”
Joshua had approached with the mindset of a commander.
He ended the encounter facedown as a servant.
And that is the image I want you to remember.
Not a powerful leader standing proudly with his sword.
But a surrendered man bowing before the authority of the LORD.
Because before Joshua could lead Israel into battle, he needed to remember who truly commanded the army.
And before we can faithfully follow Jesus, we must stop treating Him as an accessory to the lives we have already decided to live.
He is not a mascot for our ambitions.
He is not a weapon for our personal arguments.
He is not obligated to endorse every decision we make.
He is Lord.
And the astonishing beauty of the Gospel is that this holy Lord did not abandon sinners to their rebellion.
He came to save.
He bore our sins.
He rose victorious.
And He still calls people to repent, believe, and follow Him.
So if your life feels like a battlefield right now, do not mistake surrender to Christ for defeat.
You may still have difficult conversations ahead.
You may still need to seek forgiveness.
You may still need to rebuild what sin has damaged.
You may still face a tomorrow that frightens you.
But you do not have to face it while pretending you are your own savior.
Bow before Jesus.
Trust His Word.
Receive His grace.
Walk in obedience.
And remember that the God who met Joshua before Jericho is not limited by the walls that terrify human beings.
The same Scriptures that tell us of Joshua's encounter also lead us to the greater hope of Christ's finished work.
That is where our confidence belongs.
Not in the strength of our grip on God.
But in the faithfulness of the Savior who holds His people fast.
So tonight, when the noise fades and no one is watching, perhaps your most important prayer will not be, “Jesus, please take my side.”
Perhaps it will be:
“Jesus, I surrender. Teach me to stand where You want me to stand.”
And if this message has brought something hidden into the light, do not let the moment disappear into another scroll.
Respond to the Lord in prayer.
Return to His Word.
Seek the help of faithful believers where you need it.
And remember that the invitation to grace is not the end of discipleship.
It is the beginning of a life transformed by Jesus Christ.
The walls of Jericho were not Joshua's greatest lesson; before the walls ever fell, a warrior had to learn how to kneel.
